data.title: McMahon has a chance to lock in charter school opportunities
data.description:
Recent primary elections delivered a reminder of how temporary good policy can be. A bevy of candidates competing for congressional seats oppose providing public support for expansive education opportunities outside traditional education, including the 35 year-old reform called charter schools, which has historically enjoyed bi-partisan congressional support.

And in an age where student proficiency is widely understood to be in crisis, the nation can ill-afford to neglect any opportunity to improve it.

That is where Education Secretary Linda McMahon, working with Congress, has an opportunity to lock in efforts to improve student achievement. A new state-by-state scorecard reveals that states with strong charter school laws not only improve achievement but are responsible for the majority of the new and growing innovative public schools that chartering codifies in state law.

Understanding that opportunity, the Congress created in 1997 an initiative to incentivize states passing laws that give teachers, parents, and community leaders the freedom to build and run their own public schools.

Sponsored by the late Rep. Frank Riggs (R-Calif.) in the House and Sen. Joe Lieberman (D-Conn.) in the Senate, it was signed into law by President Bill Clinton. It created Public Charter School Grant Program at a time when more than two dozen states had already enacted laws making charter schools possible.

Federal start-up funding was supposed to add momentum by rewarding states that encouraged the creation of charters and gave them a level of independence and freedom to operate. And it worked that way for a while, until overzealous lawmakers, regulators and even some charter school advocates backed changes, and the competition for limited dollars became more about meeting various regulatory benchmarks than supporting operational freedom.

For example, Connecticut, which ranks at the bottom of the scorecard, received $24.5 million in 2022. Although those funds did pass through to one charter school, the state also funded an agency whose leadership is hostile to charter schools opening and denies charter schools equitable funding.

California received the largest grant in 2024, despite having passed a law that restricts charter schools to district approvals. Rhode Island, which earns a D-minus on the scorecard and ranks 45th nationally, has a statutory cap on new charter schools and one of the most centralized approval processes in the country.

Although great leaders can change the trajectory of non-entitlement-related education programs more easily with funding decisions, equality of public support for public charter schools should not be subject to political winds.

Since she has been in leadership, Secretary Linda McMahon’s department has made decisions more aligned to the law’s intent. Major awards in fiscal 2025 went to states that have maintained and even improved their strong charter school laws over time, such as Ohio, North Carolina, and Iowa.

But here’s the rub: These decisions are based on who is in charge and on regulators, not on the original intent of the law. Without codifying the law’s original intent, the states and the schools themselves are subjected to choices that a future secretary or future legislative majority could reverse without changing a single word of the law.

Meanwhile, three pro-charter members of Congress have all introduced bills this year to isolate and favor certain kinds of programs as part of the overall charter school grant program. Unfortunately, they are undermining their own intended result — more and better charter school laws at the state level that foster more and better education opportunities for kids.

That is why the principles of the original law need to become a requirement, not a choice, ensuring that Washington is not telling states how to spend their funds, but giving them a clear pathway to receive funds if they demonstrate their law meets the proven measures of what makes a great law.

My organization’s national charter law ranking and scorecard is a great instruction manual that can help build the right standard directly into how the charter school grant competition is scored and structured. It identifies what a strong charter law actually looks like — independent authorizers, real operational autonomy, funding that follows students and room for good schools to grow. State by state, it points out what is still missing.

Before federal dollars go out the door, the Education Department should return to the question Congress intended it to ask in 1997: Does this state’s law actually let charter schools be charter schools? The scorecard provides the answer, but Congress needs to ensure the principles are codified.

In addition to executing in this way, McMahon can use her bully pulpit to champion states that have done the hard work of building strong charter laws. She can also press those that haven’t, starting with her home state, to remove the barriers keeping schools from opening and growing, and make sure Washington rewards freedom rather than bureaucracy.

Jeanne Allen is founder and CEO of the Center for Education Reform and author of “The Education Avengers: Why and How A New Class of Heroes Is Fighting America’s Biggest Battle.”

data.title: Ossoff: 'Compromised' Trump won't regulate AI
data.description:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) on Monday said President Trump will likely not heed calls from technology leaders to implement guardrails on the development of artificial intelligence (AI) because of his family’s investments in the industry. 

The Georgia Democrat pointed to venture capitalist firm 1789 Capital, where Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, and its investments in AI.

“They’ve invested heavily in AI labs. They’ve invested heavily in data centers,” Ossoff told MS Now’s Lawrence O’Donnell. “So, the first family has a financial stake in this industry, and as a result, the president of the United States is compromised.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The president earlier Monday waived aside concerns raised by current and former employees of AI companies about the potential dangers of the emerging tech.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A has that, in spades!” he wrote Monday Truth Social post. 

The criticism follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s announcement of a plan to slow the pace of AI development to allow for proper safeguards to be developed and implemented. 

Trump, who is set to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week in Washington, cited U.S. competition with China on AI development in a separate post as justification to move forward with new technologies.

“President Xi, of China, just announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future,” he wrote, calling the worries about the dangers of the technology “a HOAX.”

“AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­— Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet,” the president continued. “It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!”

AI is expected to play a part in the discussions between the two leaders at the upcoming bilateral summit. 

Xi is reportedly bringing a large delegation of Chinese business leaders with him to the U.S., although it is unclear which industries will be represented by this group, according to Reuters. 

When Trump visited Beijing for a bilateral summit in May, he brought a group of American business and technology executives, including Apple CEO Tim Cook and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. 

Ossoff, who is running for reelection for his Senate seat in Georgia, called on voters to make their discontent with the president’s stance on AI known at the ballot box. 

“We already know that Donald Trump is a dangerously corrupt and incompetent man,” the senator said. “The question is what we’re going to do about it.”

data.title: With Lonnie Bunch's ouster, Trump chills free speech at the Smithsonian
data.description:
The Smithsonian Institution is a group of museums, education and research centers, created by Congress as a trust in 1846 “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.” About 62 percent of its funding comes from the federal government. The Smithsonian is supposed to be independent of the executive branch. A bipartisan board of regents runs the show. 

The Smithsonian’s first Black chieftain, Lonnie G. Bunch III 73, announced his retirement last week after more than seven years in the institution’s top job. Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, lauded Bunch for “excellence in the telling of our nation’s story,” stating that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.”  

The truth is Trump forced Bunch out of his job, heralding a tectonic shift in institutional purpose.  

Over nearly 40 years in various roles at the Smithsonian, Bunch proved himself as an effective advocate and diplomat, and an incredible fundraiser. As the institution’s guiding spirit, he was also a forceful voice on race, particularly after the 2017 Charlottesville incident and George Floyd’s 2020 Minneapolis murder. 

Bunch is a man of considerable soft-spoken warmth. I met him in New York last June when he was honored by the conservative Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History for his contributions to history, education and scholarship. He left an indelible impression. The son of two teachers, his love of history was palpable as he said eloquently, “there is nothing more powerful than a people, than a nation, steeped in its history. And there’s nothing more noble than honoring all our ancestors by remembering.”  

What obviously led to Bunch’s abrupt resignation was Trump on his case. Out of some perverse desire for political cleansing of artistic expression, Trump waged a chilling campaign on the Smithsonian to purge what he called “improper ideology,”  going so far as to threaten the institution’s federal funding and challenge its autonomy. 

Bunch told the New York Times it was not the Trump freeze-out that spurred his departure, but admitted that at times, his role had been “stressful”. 

“When you’re Black in America, you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right?” he said. “You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table.” 

Trump’s drive to gut the Smithsonian began in March 2025 with an executive order that accused the institution of spouting a “divisive” and “race centered” message. The White House subsequently identified exhibits it found objectionable, principally targeting discussions of race, slavery, immigration and transgender identity. 

The sparks flew further in May 2025 when Trump said he had fired Kim Sajet, longtime director of the National Portrait Gallery, calling her highly partisan and a supporter of diversity, equity and inclusion. The Smithsonian’s regents pushed back. After a tense meeting, they publicly affirmed that personnel decisions belonged to Bunch, with oversight by the board. Sajet resigned four days later, saying her departure was the best way to serve the institution.  

Pressure soon expanded beyond personnel. Trump went ballistic posting on social media in August 2025 that the institution “is OUT OF CONTROL,” and only discusses “how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been.” 

“We have the “HOTTEST” Country in the World, and we want people to talk about it, including in our Museums,” he added.  

This spring, Bunch said he was proud of what the Smithsonian had achieved under his leadership despite the barrage of Trump attacks. “Nothing can take that away,” he said. “So, I’m trying to make sure I don’t let this moment steal my joy.”

The White House next produced a July 4 report about the National Museum of American History that accused its director of “radical activist ideology” and charges the museum with undermining “faith in American institutions.” The board called for its 21 museums to review their content for partisanship or bias. But the administration began its own review of exhibitions, wall text and social media to assess “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals.”  

After the report, the salvos continued. Museum director Anthea M. Hartig came under fire at two congressional hearings. Trump ordered posting of warning signs to convey his view that the museum did not accurately reflect American history. The signs never appeared.

Later, the White House escalated again, with a 162-page report accusing the National Museum of American History of portraying the American story as one of “regret, tragedy, and shame.”  

Bunch, who generally avoided publicly confronting Trump, forcefully pushed back. He told Smithsonian employees the report was “not a fair characterization” of the museum and said its work remained driven by “scholarship, accuracy, and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story.” 

“America is not afraid of its own history,” Bunch said. “My job is always to help the Smithsonian tell complicated stories that really allow us to understand the fullness of the American experience.” The institution’s 180-year-old history is “a reservoir…for understanding of science, of history, of art.”  

“For me, it is really building on the Smithsonian’s long history of saying, ‘No matter what, we will be independent.’”  

Bunch plans to depart by the end of the year.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

data.title: Watch live: Patel testifies on FBI oversight
data.description:
FBI Director Kash Patel is testifying Tuesday before the Senate Judiciary Committee on oversight of the federal law enforcement agency.

Patel is likely to face questions over a series of personnel shake-ups and controversies surrounding his conduct and use of government resources for travel. The FBI chief has defended his actions against criticism.

data.title: Chris Land: Staff director, Senate Banking subcommittee on digital assets
data.description:
Chris Land’s journey to becoming the lead negotiator on a major Senate cryptocurrency bill started far from the halls of Congress. 

Land, who serves as the staff director for the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Subcommittee on Digital Assets, was working in the Wyoming Legislature after law school, not planning to work on crypto, when the issue fell into his lap.  

“I was the only person in the Wyoming Legislature that knew what Bitcoin was in 2017,” he quipped.

As a staff attorney in the state Legislature, Land had a hand in drafting Wyoming’s early crypto and digital asset laws, which he said gave him a “big head start on a lot of the issues Congress was going to consider over the last few years.” 

He joined Sen. Cynthia Lummis’s (R-Wyo.) office in 2021, serving as general counsel and later staff director when the senator was tapped to chair the digital assets subcommittee in 2025. 

Crypto has become a priority during the second Trump administration, with two pieces of legislation dominating the conversation.

The GENIUS Act, which created a regulatory framework for dollar-backed digital tokens known as stablecoins, cleared Congress and was signed into law by President Trump last year. The Clarity Act, which seeks to develop rules for the rest of the market, remains under negotiation in the Senate.  

Land described the process of hashing out the bills as a “daily grind” and an “adventure” involving dozens of late nights, calls on Christmas Eve and his birthday, and thousands of hours of staff time. 

“We’ve kind of been in fire drill mode for the last year, more or less, on trying to get these bills through,” he said.

When the Clarity Act ultimately advanced out of the Senate Banking panel earlier this year — after a markup cancellation and a months-long fight between the banking and crypto industries — both Lummis and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) praised Land’s work. 

“I can’t say enough about your dedication to this,” Lummis said at the May markup. “As I’ve said to Chris many times, we’re the dogs that caught the tire.” 

Tillis joked at the time that Lummis and her staff deserved a “long weekend,” adding, “They all do, and especially Chris.” 

“Staff are supposed to be anonymous most of the time,” Land told The Hill, adding, “But it really meant a lot to me. It was an unforgettable memory that I’ll treasure for my entire life.”

data.title: Trump's tariffs on Canada could cost him several red states
data.description:
If you were a conspiracy theorist, you might think President Trump is trying his best to get Republican candidates defeated in the November midterm elections. That’s because the tariffs he recently imposed on Canadian imports, and Canada’s response by imposing tariffs on U.S. imports, hit several red states very hard, which is fueling voters’ anger.

Trump is apparently upset with the U.S.-Canada trade imbalance. Americans buy more imports from Canada ($454 billion in 2025) than Canadians buy from the U.S. ($426 billion). That’s a $27 billion trade deficit. But the United States has nearly nine times the population of Canada. Of course, Americans buy more.

Canada is America’s second biggest trading partner. Sales and jobs in both countries depend on a vibrant cross-border trading economy, which Trump’s tariffs could undermine.

A recent assessment by the Visual Capitalist highlights 23 states that get most of their imports from Canada. Among the states with closely watched elections are Maine, which gets 68.7 percent of it imports from Canada, Alaska (40.7 percent), Minnesota (33.5 percent), Iowa (26.6 percent), and Ohio (18.7 percent).

But trade is a two-way street. It’s not just the increased costs — up to 50 percent more — U.S. companies, small businesses (like farms) and consumers must pay for Canadian imports. There are also U.S.-made products and services that Canadians may decide not to buy from the United States because the of the tariffs Canada, in response, imposed on imports from the United States. The Visual Capitalist’s newly released map outlines the states hardest hit.

The biggest state exporters to Canada are Ohio (exporting $2.3 billion a year) and Pennsylvania ($1.8 billion). Are there important elections in those states that could make the difference in whether Republicans retain the House of Representatives and the Senate?

Wisconsin’s also on the list ($1.4 billion), as well as Michigan and Indiana (both at $1.3 billion). And even though Maine only exports $453 million to Canada, that’s a lot for a small state — and with one of the most important Senate races for Republicans in the country.

In fact, Canada is a huge trading partner all across the heartland, where Republican support tends to be strongest — or should I say “tended” to be strongest? Iowa sells $529 million to Canada, North Carolina $601 million, and Minnesota $594 million. And how about $908 million in very important Georgia.

Voters in the most affected states are taking notice, and that’s going to weigh on Republicans’ election chances.

National Public Radio has been holding focus groups around the country made up of swing voters who voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but switched to Trump in 2024. These are the voters who put Trump over the finish line in 2024. Most of them are not happy. As NPR reporter Mara Liasson observes, “This is a consistent echo across all our focus groups — No. 1 issue, affordability, cost of living.” Trump’s tariffs negatively impact both, and where we find Trump’s worst polling numbers.

Just consider Maine, where Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins’ polling has consistently trailed her Democratic opponent by a few points. She has understandably criticized Trump’s tariff policies. Collins may outperform the polls and win in November — she did in her last election in 2020. But if she does, it will be in spite of Trump and his tariffs, not because of him.

In Iowa, there is an open Senate seat, as Republican Joni Ernst steps down. Iowa has been trending red for several years, but the Democratic Senate candidate, Josh Turek, began pulling ahead of Republican candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson in the last two weeks — about the time U.S.-Canadian trade talks collapsed. And the Democratic candidate for governor is well ahead of the Republican.

In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed by the Republican governor last year to replace Vice President JD Vance, is running 5 points behind his Democratic challenger, former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

And how about that all-important open Senate seat in Michigan, one of the states most closely connected with Canada. The latest poll at RealClearPolling has progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leading Republican Mike Rogers by 3 points.

All of these Senate elections, and many more, such as North Carolina and Alaska, are winnable for Republicans — or at least they were. But Trump’s tariff policies are dragging them down. Republican candidates either must defend Trump’s tariffs on Canada or criticize them. If candidates defend them, voters complain; if they criticize them, Trump complains — loudly.

The most puzzling part is that if Trump were determined to pick a trade fight with Canada, he could have easily waited until after November. He chose to do it weeks away from a critical election, which makes you wonder if the conspiracy theorists are right.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.

data.title: Tom Rust: Chief counsel and staff director, House Ethics Committee
data.description:
For nearly two decades, Tom Rust has worked behind the scenes to help police the conduct of lawmakers.

Rust joined the House Ethics Committee in 2009 after nearly a decade in private legal practice. He quickly moved up the ranks, serving as senior counsel and acting director of investigations before taking the role of staff director in 2014.

Today, Rust oversees roughly 30 staffers working across the committee’s advice, investigations and financial disclosure offices. He also advises the committee’s 10 members, who are evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

His work has included some of the House’s most high-profile ethics investigations.

Asked about the most interesting case he has encountered, Rust pointed to the investigation into former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.), whom the House voted to expel in 2023. Santos was sentenced to a seven-year prison term after he pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, but he was released from prison last year after President Trump commuted his sentence.

“There were just so many different issues there,” Rust said. “It was a wide-ranging case that involved allegations of criminal misconduct. It involved interactions with an ongoing criminal investigation. It was very high-profile.”

Rust said one of the most rewarding parts of his job is working with the committee members.

“If you took the transcript of our committee meeting and you took the names off the transcript, you oftentimes have trouble finding out which party somebody is in because our discussions are — they are very serious,” he said. “Our members all take it very seriously, and they are not particularly partisan in the room, which is great.”

That dynamic is also central to how Rust responds to accusations that the committee is partisan. Investigators frequently face criticism from the people they scrutinize, he said, but the committee’s evenly divided membership and nonpartisan staff provide an important safeguard.

“The best way to address any criticism of your work is just let your work speak for itself and do the best work possible,” Rust said.

The biggest challenge, he added, is the committee’s confidentiality. Because much of its work happens behind closed doors, outsiders can sometimes misunderstand its process.

For Rust, the mission remains the draw. He expects to remain with the committee for at least the next few years.

 He said protecting the integrity of the House is “a valuable thing.”

data.title: The latest court ruling against deportations ignores precedent and won't hold up
data.description:
A federal judge has declared two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act unconstitutional in a ninety-page opinion that never mentions the Supreme Court cases upholding exactly such a law.

Recently, in Stanford Daily v. Rubio, Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California held that the government may not deport foreign visitors or revoke their visas based on “protected speech.” She declared the law’s foreign-policy removal and visa-revocation provisions unconstitutional to that extent.

Her opinion holds that noncitizens enjoy First Amendment rights to the same extent as citizens. For that proposition, it leans on the Ninth Circuit’s 1995 decision in American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee v. Reno. That case arose from the government’s effort to deport members and supporters of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

Here is what Wise’s opinion leaves out: That very litigation all the way to the Supreme Court, where the ruling she cited was overturned. The government won the case.

In Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, the Supreme Court held that Congress had stripped the lower courts of jurisdiction over such claims. Justice Antonin Scalia wrote for the court that “[a]s a general matter,” an alien “unlawfully in this country has no constitutional right to assert selective enforcement as a defense against his deportation,” and that the executive “should not have to disclose its ‘real’ reasons” for deporting particular foreign nationals.

The plaintiffs in this new case are lawfully present, so a careful court might have distinguished the case on that ground. But Wise did not do so. Her opinion cites the Ninth Circuit decision four times and completely omits the Supreme Court’s last word in the same case.

The Supreme Court’s ruling is part of a much larger jurisprudential pattern. In 1904, Turner v. Williams upheld the exclusion of an English anarchist for his advocacy. Chief Justice Melville Fuller wrote that governments “cannot be denied the power of self-preservation.” Wise failed to cite or acknowledge this case.

In Harisiades v. Shaughnessy, which might be the closest case to the current one, the Supreme Court in 1952 upheld the deportation of lawful permanent residents, one of whom had been in the country for thirty-eight years, due to Communist Party membership. The same First Amendment objection was rejected.

In Mathews v. Diaz, the Supreme Court in 1976 explained that in immigration, “Congress regularly makes rules that would be unacceptable if applied to citizens.” Wise failed even to cite this case, let alone confront its reasoning.

Another more recent case missing from Wise’s opinion is Trump v. Hawaii, which in 2018 upheld a statute allowing presidents to bar aliens they find “detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The court’s opinion states that the law “exudes deference to the president in every clause.”

Wise also fails to mention or confront or name the doctrine — “plenary power” — that has governed this area of law since the nineteenth century.

Contrary to what some say, foreigners lawfully among us do indeed have free-speech rights. The Supreme Court said as much in its 1945 decision in Bridges v. Wixon. However — and this is very important — removal from the U.S. is not a punishment.

In the Reno case mentioned above, the Supreme Court explained that a deported alien “is not being punished” for his conduct but “is merely being held to the terms under which he was admitted.” The court located the limit in the nature of the removal power rather than in any discount on the alien’s rights. A visa is an invitation, and this country’s invitations have always come with the understanding that the host, not the guest, decides when the arrangement has soured.

Nor did the host act on a whim. The referral letters and determination memoranda quoted in the opinion gave two reasons for the government’s actions. One was conduct “creating a hostile environment for Jewish students,” and the other was conduct “indicating support for a designated terrorist organization.”

Judge Wise recites both but weighs neither. Congress wrote the second reason into the statute books: Any alien who “endorses or espouses terrorist activity” is inadmissible and, under a companion provision, deportable. Yet Judge Wise, hunting for gentler alternatives to the provision she struck, oddly cites the statutory language as “speech-neutral.”

Yet the Supreme Court, for its part, held in 2010, in Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, that Congress may imprison even American citizens if they engage in advocacy coordinated with designated terrorist groups. Under Wise’s ruling, the same government may not so much as un-invite a foreign guest who applauds a terrorist group’s massacres. The hierarchy is clearly upside down.

Wise declared the deportation provision unconstitutionally vague because it turns on the Secretary of State’s personal determination that a foreigner’s presence compromises “a compelling United States foreign policy interest.” Her supporting authorities are two district-court decisions: One that was reversed by the Third Circuit in 1996, the other which was vacated by that court this year. It’s not that Wise is unaware of this: Her opinion merely nods to both outcomes in a footnote and then marches on.

Meanwhile, Matter of Ruiz-Massieu, the 1996 Board of Immigration Appeals decision squarely upholding this provision against the same challenges, is acknowledged only as an example of enforcement history — its holding is never engaged. Judge Wise also quotes Secretary Rubio’s assurance that nobody loses a visa for protesting paper straws as proof that no standard exists. But a standard that separates paper straws from Hamas is not standardless. Most Americans could administer such a thing in their sleep, which may be why Congress assigned it to a cabinet officer rather than a faculty lounge.

There was an off-ramp for Wise, but she drove past it. Under Rust v. Sullivan and Justice Brandeis’s canonical rules in Ashwander v. TVA, a court facing constitutional doubts must first look for a saving construction. Yet “constitutional avoidance” appears nowhere in Wise’s opinion. Invalidating an act of Congress, even in part, is supposed to be a last resort, but Wise never even bothered to try another route.

Wise’s ruling is already being paraded by activists as vindication for Mahmoud Khalil — not least by Khalil himself. But it is nothing of the sort. It removes no one from proceedings, releases no one, vacates no removal order, and cancels no visa revocation. It also binds no other court. A district court opinion is precedent for nobody. Khalil, the Columbia graduate and green-card holder whose March 2025 arrest opened this drama, is not a party to the case, so the decision does not touch the order governing him.

Last September, an immigration judge ordered him removed on a separate ground: willful omissions from his green-card application, including his service with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency and his work in the Syria office of the British Embassy in Beirut. No ruling about protected speech can launder a false application.

The Stanford Daily has been here before. In the 1970s, after police searched its newsroom, the paper won a case in the district court and the Ninth Circuit, only to be reversed by the Supreme Court in Zurcher v. Stanford Daily. Every journalism student reads that case with a shudder. The Justice Department has sixty days to notice an appeal, but it shouldn’t take nearly that long to make its decision.

The Ninth Circuit should reverse Wise’s unwise ruling. If it prefers its own 1995 opinion to the way the Supreme Court ended that case in 1999, it can take its chances and remind everyone how that last Stanford Daily experiment ended.

The guest list of the U.S. belongs to its hosts. It is time the courts handed it back.

Mark Goldfeder is a former law professor and director of the National Jewish Advocacy Center.

data.title: Kamela White: Democratic clerk, Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security
data.description:
Kamela White sees that numbers can tell a story — or be used to hide one.

As a clerk for Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security, White plays a role in shaping federal policy through government funding.

She said her biggest goal under the Trump administration has been to work for accountability as the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has been given unprecedented levels of funding with few strings attached.

White, 51, noted that the DHS has gotten more than a trillion dollars in federal funding amid “the evisceration of any sort of oversight.”

Some of that shifted, however, with the adoption of the 2026 budget more than a year into President Trump’s term and as GOP senators found they were also getting silence on their requests to the administration.

“I think a lot of the lack of information sharing, the lack of answering questions, it wasn’t just our questions; they weren’t answering the majority’s questions either. So there’s a shared frustration with the inability to get information that I think really helped us to have a lot of common ground,” she said.

“Otherwise, we’re just like, ‘What’d you spend that $190 billion on?’ Because they didn’t have to report a penny of it.”

White spent years at the Office of Management and Budget and served at U.S. Customs and Border Protection. She made the switch during former President Obama’s era after helping build out predictive analytics data to assess what personnel levels would be needed to respond to expected flows along the border and at ports of entry, shifting how Congress decided to fund the agency.

“What changed was you weren’t arguing over the numbers anymore,” she said, prompting the agency to realize it hadn’t been “telling our story.”

“You have a better opportunity to build that common ground if you’re able to introduce trusted data.”

Under Trump, White has also been part of the team investigating how immigration funding has been spent, uncovering that the DHS bought 12 planes without authorization for the purchases from Congress and paid above market rate for warehouses officials planned to turn into detention centers.

“By default, you are setting policy with funding,” she said, noting that some funding has strict parameters around its use.

She also said the committee’s Democrats were able to “restore some of the changes the administration put in place, and make it harder for them to either stonewall or not respond” to oversight.

“No oversight on money is a dangerous thing,” she said.

data.title: Wyndee Parker: National security adviser, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)
data.description:
No two days are the same for Wyndee Parker.

As national security adviser to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Parker is responsible for overseeing the activities of all of the lower chamber’s national security committees, including Armed Services, Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, Homeland Security and their Appropriations counterparts.

She also works with the executive branch and its corresponding agencies that make up the entire intelligence community, including the CIA, National Security Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department, State Department and some elements of the Department of Homeland Security.

Day to day, she helps ensure information is flowing to Congress and lawmakers and their staff are “kept as informed as they should be about all of the executive branch activities, operations, etc.,” often working with the National Security Council to ensure that the right briefings come together.

On top of that, Parker ensures Jeffries is prepared for “a lot” of meetings with foreign dignitaries and senior executive branch officials, and she helps work on and review legislation that moves out of committees and onto the House floor, such as the National Defense Authorization Act — one of the largest bills Congress passes annually.

The role is a study in multitasking.

“No day is like any other,” she said.

Parker admits she was “a little skeptical” when she came to Capitol Hill 25 years ago to serve as counsel on the House Intelligence Committee. That was a few years after receiving her law degree from Ohio State University and working in the office of general counsels for both the CIA and FBI. 

“My supervisor at the time told me ‘you know, no day is like any other day that’s gone before.’ … A couple decades later, I’m saying the same thing said to me,” she said, attributing it to the nature of national security work. 

“The world is so dynamic. It keeps us definitely motivated and kind of energized,” Parker said before adding that the phone rings “too often, I should say, between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m.”

Prior to working for Jeffries, Parker was with another senior member of the Democratic Party for nearly 15 years: former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), also serving as her national security adviser.

When she’s not up to her neck in national security matters, Parker said she relishes spending time with her husband and two children. 

“I cherish those moments,” she said.
